title: Packet
text: Marshfield Zoning Board of Appeals 870 Moraine Street, Marshfield, MA 02050 Tuesday, December 8, 2026 at 6:30 P.M. NOTICE OF PUBLIC HEARING Pursuant to Chapter 2 of the Acts of 2023 dated March 29, 2023, An Act Relative to Extending Certain COVID 19 Measures Adopted During the State of Emergency regarding suspending certain provisions of the Open Meeting Law, G. L. c. 30A §18, the Town of Marshfield’s Zoning Board of Appeals Meeting will be conducted both in-person and via remote participation. For this meeting, members of the public may attend in-person or may participate remotely, a hybrid form of meeting, also utilizing the ZOOM Meeting Instructions (video and phone in instructions) listed below. The public may also view the meeting by viewing the Town of Marshfield’s government access channels: Verizon (Chanel 35) and Comcast (Channel 15). Every effort will be made to ensure that members and the public can adequately access the proceedings to the best of our technical abilities; and, despite our best efforts, this meeting may be viewed as a video recording on Marshfield Community Television website (marshfieldtv.org) and a transcript or other comprehensive record of the meeting will be available as soon as possible after the meeting. Please note that while an option for remote attendance and/or participation is being provided as a courtesy to the public, the meeting/hearing will not be suspended or terminated if technological problems interrupt the virtual broadcast, unless required by law. If participating remotely, you must have microphone or you will not be able to speak. You must have camera if you want to see video. A Public Hearing will be held by the MARSHFIELD ZONING BOARD OF APPEALS on Tuesday, December 8, 2026 at 6:30 P.M. to consider the following: #26-62: Kirsten J. Banks – The Petitioner is seeking a Special Permit in accordance with §§ 305-9.02 and 305-10.12 of the Marshfield Municipal Code to construct a covered porch along the left side of the existing nonconforming-dwelling. The proposed porch will measure 16’ x 8’, within 36’ of frontage on the property located at 144 Spring Street, further identified on the Marshfield Assessors’ Maps as being on parcel D19-04-05 and is located in the R-1 Zoning District. #26-63: Joseph & Catherine Duffey – The Petitioner is seeking a Special Permit in accordance with §§ 305-9.02 and 305-10.12 of the Marshfield Municipal Code to alter and extend the first and second floor to the existing nonconforming single-family dwelling on the nonconforming property located at 93 Bay Avenue, further identified on the Marshfield Assessors’ Maps as being on parcel M04-19-08 and is located in the R-3 Zoning District and the Floodplain Overlay District. #26-64: Eric & Mary Murphy – The Petitioner is seeking a Special Permit in accordance with §§ 305-9.02 and 305-10.12 and a Variance in accordance with §§ 305-10.11 and 305-6.01 of the Marshfield Municipal Code to permit the demolition of the existing multifamily dwelling and construct a new elevated, pile-supported multifamily dwelling containing two rental dwellings on the property located at 236 Ocean Street, further identified on the Marshfield Assessors’ Maps as being on parcel N07-01-08 and is located in the R-3 Zoning District and the Floodplain Overlay District. The Petitioners and all interested parties are advised to check the Town website and/or Zoning Board of Appeals homepage for additional information and details. Brian Murphy, Chair Grover Hensley, Jr., Vice Chair Stephen Lynch Eric Murphy Mary Anne Brogan Larry Keane, Clerk Mack Brothers

Susan M Galvin 11/10/2026 03:53 pm Posting Authority AGENDA (Must be included at time of posting) In Massachusetts, Governor Healey signed a bill on March 28, 2025, extending the temporary provisions of the Open Meeting Law, allowing public bodies to continue holding remote meetings and providing "adequate, alternative" access until June 30, 2027. Hearing upon the Application of Erin Conti at 43 Hazel Street, dated October 28, 2026, seeking a Special Permit to build an 8 foot by 42 foot, front side second-story addition, an 8 foot by 30 foot second story left side addition, a new 8-foot-wide attic dormer, and a new 5 foot by 7 foot covered front porch to the existing structure. The property is located in a Residence C Zoning District. As the proposed project would increase the existing nonconformity of the structure, per the Milton Zoning Bylaw, Article IX, Section 275-4.1 (B) a Special Permit from the ZBA is required to proceed. In addition, the proposed front porch would have a 14-foot setback when 20 feet is required per the Milton Zoning Bylaw Article X, Section 275.10-2 C (Front Yards). Therefore, the permit was denied. All as therein set forth in said Application and plans on file with the Board and open to public inspection. To view files. title: Notice of Public Hearing, 10 Cottage Street 12-15-2026
text: By Town of Westborough at 3:27 pm, Nov 09, 2026 TOWN OF WESTBOROUGH OFFICE OF THE PLANNING BOARD APPLICATION FOR SPECIAL PERMIT AND SITE PLAN REVIEW In accordance with the provisions of M.G.L. Chapter 40A, Section 9 and Sections 3.1, 4.7 and 5.3 and Attachment I (Use Regulation Schedule) of the Town of Westborough Zoning Bylaw, the Westborough Planning Board will hold a public hearing on Tuesday, December 15, 2026 at 6:30PM on application record no. 26-03301, requesting a Special Permit and Site Plan Review. The application, submitted by Daniel Peirce, Trustee of 10 Cottage Street Realty Trust, proposes four (4) two-family residential buildings, providing a total of eight (8) homes at 10 Cottage Street. The application includes a request for relief from the minimum front-yard setback requirement of ten (10) feet from the front property line or fifty (50) feet from the street centerline, proposing a setback of five (5) feet from the front property line and twenty-one and one-half (21.5) feet from the street centerline. The public hearing will be held in the Great Hall of the Forbes Municipal Building, 45 West Main Street, Westborough, MA. Please see the Calendar on the Town of Westborough Homepage (posted 48 hours prior to the public hearing) for additional information. To access the application and any submitted documents, please go to our online permitting system, PermitPro (https://westborough.patriotpermitpro.com/) and search the above-referenced record number. Records are also available for review in the Westborough Planning Board Office at 45 West Main St., Westborough, MA during regular business hours. Persons unable to attend may submit comments in writing to the Westborough Planning Board in advance of the public hearing. WESTBOROUGH PLANNING BOARD Hazel Nourse, Chair

title: Tax Classification Public Hearing
text: TAX CLASSIFICATION PUBLIC HEARING MONDAY, DECEMBER 7, 2026 7:30 P.M. PUBLIC HEARING NOTICE On Monday, December 7, 2026 at 7:30 p.m., the Select Board of the Town of Longmeadow will conduct the Annual Tax Classification hearing in accordance with M.G.L., Ch. 40 § 56 to determine the percentage share of the tax levy to be borne by each class of property, relative to setting the Fiscal Year 2027 tax rate(s). The hearing will be held at 231 Maple Road in the Greenwood Conference Room. The hearing will include a presentation by Maria Cataldo, Principal Assessor, outlining the options available under Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 40 § 56. All concerned taxpayers who wish to present their views orally are encouraged to attend. If you wish to access this meeting via Zoom, the link to the Select Board Meeting will be provided on the Town’s website on Wednesday, December 2, 2026. If there are any questions about the hearing, please contact the Assessors’ Office at 565-4115.

text: CONSERVATION COMMISSION MEETING December 1, 2026 TIME 7:00 PM Meetings are live streamed on Andover46.com Broadcast on Comcast Channel 22 and Verizon Channel 45 Pursuant to S.2475 “An Act Relative to Extending Certain COVID-19 Measures Adopted During the State of Emergency”, which was enacted into law on June 16, 2021, and which was extended by legislation enacted on March 28, 2025, this meeting of the Andover Conservation Commission will be conducted via remote participation to the greatest extent possible. The virtual meeting will be streamed live on Andover46.com and broadcast on Comcast Channel 22, and Verizon Channel 45. Members of the public wishing to attend the public meeting may call or email the Conservation office at (978)623-8630 or CDPConservation@andoverma.us to obtain the link to access the meeting, in compliance with the Guidance on Holding Meeting Pursuant to the Act Extending Certain COVID-19 Measures. Members of the public who wish to communicate to the meeting can do so by emailing CDPCONSERVATION@ANDOVERMA.US. Residents are encouraged to email their questions or comments ahead of the meeting — however, staff will be available to present the Andover Conservation Commission with questions and comments received during the meeting. Please include your name and address with your question or comment. Every effort will be made to ensure that the public can adequately access the proceedings in real time via technological means. In the event that we are unable to do so despite our best efforts, we will post to the Town’s website an audio or video recording, transcript, or other comprehensive record of the proceedings as soon as possible after the meeting. Persons may also call the Conservation Department at (978) 623-8630. title: Conservation Commission Public Hearing Notice
text: Falmouth Conservation Commission 59 Town Hall Square, Falmouth, Massachusetts 02540 (508) 495-7445 • concom@falmouthma.gov FALMOUTH CONSERVATION COMMISSION PUBLIC HEARING NOTICE December 2, 2026 at 7:00 p.m. The Falmouth Conservation Commission will hold a public hearing under Section 40, Chapter 131 of the general laws of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts Wetlands Protection Act and/or the Town of Falmouth Wetlands Protection Bylaw. Covid protocols have been extended to allow for continued expanded remote participation, the public meeting of the Falmouth Conservation Commission shall be physically closed to the public to avoid group congregation. Public access to this meeting shall be provided in the following manner: 1. The meeting will be televised via Falmouth Community Television. 2. Real-time public comment can be addressed to the Conservation Commission utilizing the Zoom virtual meeting software for remote access. This application will allow users to view and participate in the meeting. Text comments submitted with the Chat function will be read into the record at the appropriate points in the meeting. a. Zoom Login instructions: i. Instructions and the meeting link for this specific meeting can be found at the following web address: http://www.falmouthma.gov/Conservation ii. Please plan on 10-15 minutes of preparation time to log in though it may be less if you have previously used Zoom on the device you will use to access this meeting. 3. Additionally public comments may be sent in advance of the meeting to concom@falmouthma.gov at least 5 hours prior to the beginning of the meeting. Documents and audio or video files may also be submitted via email. Submitted email comments and documents will be made part of the meeting record. 4. Applicants, their representatives and individuals with enforcement matters before the Conservation Commission shall appear remotely. Applicants, their representatives and individuals with enforcement matters before the Conservation Commission may contact the Conservation Department to arrange an alternative means of real time participation if unable to use the Zoom virtual meeting software. Documentary exhibits and/or visual presentations should be submitted in advance of the meeting to concom@falmouthma.gov so they may be displayed for remote public access viewing. Complete applications are available by request and will be sent via email. text: City of GREENFIELD, MASSACHUSETTS ___ PLANNING AND DEVELOPMENT Virginia Desorgher Mayor PLANNING BOARD City Hall ● 14 Court Square ● Greenfield, MA 01301 Phone 413-772-1549 ● Ella.Wise@greenfield-ma.gov ● www.greenfield-ma.gov TO: Lora Wondolowski, City Council President Members of the Greenfield City Council FROM: Jeff Sauser, Chairperson, Planning Board DATE: September 3, 2026 RE: Planning Board initiation of proposed zoning amendments to Section 200-7.2 to allow multifamily buildings to consist of more than one building per lot. At its September 3, 2026 meeting, the Planning Board, after careful consideration and deliberation, took the following vote relative to the proposed zoning amendments to Section 2007.2 to allow multifamily buildings to consist of more than one building per lot. MOTION: Moved by Moschella, seconded by Brown-Anson, and voted 5:0:0 to initiate the proposed zoning amendment as further amended below to allow multifamily buildings to consist of more than one building per lot in the Central Commercial, General Commercial, Limited Commercial, and General Industrial zoning districts. --~ 200-7.2. Multifamily dwellings. A. Special permit required. The Zoning Board of Appeals may grant a special permit for multifamily dwellings under the following procedures and requirements. Multifamily dwellings in open space/cluster developments shall also comply with the requirements of ~ 200-7.1 of this ordinance. B. Procedure. (1) Applicants shall submit seven (7) copies of an application and the proposed site plan, prepared by a registered engineer, architect, or other qualified professional, showing proposed structures, parking, drives, landscaping, topography and drainage, plus architectural elevations of all proposed buildings and any other site plan submittal requirements specified in the Site Plan, ~ 200-8.4 of this ordinance. Where the development of a Priority Development Site (PDS) requires a special permit hereunder, the aforesaid application and site plan shall be submitted simultaneously The City of Greenfield is an Affirmative Action/Equal Opportunity Employer, a designated Green Community and a recipient of the “Leading by Example” Award with any other permit application(s) required (a) by this Ordinance or (b) by the Code, generally, relating to the use or development of land, buildings or structures and not otherwise exempted by G.L. c. 43D. [Subsection 1 amended by Town Council on October 21, 2009] (2) Within ten (10) days of its receipt, one (1) copy of the application and site plan shall be forwarded by the Clerk of the Board of Appeals to the Planning Board, who shall submit a report of recommendations to the Board of Appeals within thirty (30) days. (3) The Board of Appeals shall not hold a public hearing on the application until receipt of the Planning Board report, or until forty-five (45) days has lapsed from the date of filing. Where the special permit sought hereunder is for the development of one (1) or more multifamily dwellings on a Priority Development Site (PDS), the Zoning Board of Appeals shall render a decision thereon no later than one hundred eighty (180) days from the date of submission of the application. [Subsection 3 amended by Town Council on October 21, 2009] (4) Multifamily dwellings may consist of one (1) or more buildings on one (1) lot in the Central Commercial (CC), General Commercial (GC), Limited Commercial (LC), and General Industry (GI) zoning districts. (45) Multifamily structures shall be served by a public way having sufficient width, suitable grades, and adequate construction to accommodate the increase in traffic generated by the site. (56) The site shall be designed so that access, grading, water and sewer systems, drainage, roads and sidewalks meet all applicable standards established in the Greenfield Planning Board Subdivision Regulations,1 and the specifications and standards of the Department of Public Works; no building shall be floodlit; driveways and parking areas shall be illuminated only by shielded lights not higher than fifteen (15) feet; no lighting shall cast observable shadows onto adjoining premises; major topographic changes or removal of existing trees shall be avoided and effective use shall be made of the topography, landscaping, and building placement to make maximum use of solar energy, protect the character of the environs, and protect scenic views seen from public ways. (67) Parking areas shall be screened from public ways and adjacent properties by building location, grading, fencing, or planting. Parking shall be off-street and shall provide for forward moving ingress and egress onto any traveled way. No parking area shall contain more than thirtysix (36) parking spaces. The City of Greenfield is an Affirmative Action/Equal Opportunity Employer, a designated Green Community and a recipient of the “Leading by Example” Award (78) A development phasing schedule may be established by the Board of Appeals in accordance with ~ 200-8.3. (89) If the development will not be connected to a public water or sewer system, the applicant shall submit plans for an individual water supply system and a septic system designed by a registered sanitary engineer approved by the Greenfield Board of Health and if necessary, the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Quality Engineering. No septic system serving the development shall exceed two thousand (2,000) gallons per day sewage flow as determined under 310 CMR Section 15.02, Title 5 of the State Environmental Code. More than one (1) septic system may serve the site in order to meet this requirement. (910) A special permit for multifamily dwellings shall not be granted unless the Zoning Board of Appeals finds that the requirements of ~ 200-8.3 of this ordinance have been met. --Respectfully submitted, Jeff Sauser Chairperson, Planning Board The City of Greenfield is an Affirmative Action/Equal Opportunity Employer, a designated Green Community and a recipient of the “Leading by Example” Award Official Zoning Map BERNARDSTON City of Greenfield, Massachusetts HA N HTS BARTO L MIL ! The Planning Board requests the initiation of the attached zoning amendments in order to allow residential adaptive reuse of accessory structures by Special Permit. The zoning amendment includes a new section in the “Special Regulations” article, as well as amendments to the “Use Regulations.” Recently, two local landowners have met with the Planning Director to inquire about converting existing accessory structures into residential units either for themselves or their family. The Planning Director proposed an amendment to the existing ADU ordinance to allow for ADUs larger than 900 square feet by Special Permit. However, the proposal to reconsider the ADU ordinance was met with pushback. Therefore, the draft amendment below is independent of the ADU ordinance – it is a new zoning ordinance to allow for existing accessory structures, such as barns or carriage houses, built before August 2016 to be converted into single-family homes by Special Permit. The City of Greenfield is an Affirmative Action/Equal Opportunity Employer, a designated Green Community and a recipient of the “Leading by Example” Award Note: Text with a strikethrough is text to be deleted, black bold italic text is newly proposed text. ---ARTICLE VII ~ 200-7.22. Adaptive Residential Reuse of Accessory Structures A. Purpose. The purpose of this Section is to allow the adaptive reuse of existing accessory structures, such as barns, carriage houses, garages, and other structures for residential purposes in any zoning district where residential uses are allowed. This zoning provides for adaptive residential reuse of accessory structures to accomplish the following purposes: (1) Enable homeowners to utilize existing structures on their land for rental income and alternative living options; (2) Support the maintenance of and prevent dilapidation of historical structures; (3) Increase housing options with gentle density that maintains the existing fabric of the built environment; (4) B. Ensure safe and healthy housing compliant with the Building Code. Applicability. (1) See Sections 200-4.1 through 200-4.17 and Appendix A, Table of Uses, for permitting requirements. C. Adaptive Residential Reuse Standards. The Zoning Board of Appeals, acting as the special permit granting authority (SPGA), may grant a special permit to use an existing accessory structure for single-family residential use on a lot with any number of existing dwellings, provided all of the following conditions are satisfied: (1) The accessory structure must have existed continuously since before August 2016 and have a minimum gross floor area of 900 square feet. (2) The accessory structure may be converted to no more than one dwelling unit and must be a complete, separate housekeeping unit containing both kitchen and bath. The City of Greenfield is an Affirmative Action/Equal Opportunity Employer, a designated Green Community and a recipient of the “Leading by Example” Award (3) The accessory structure may not expand in gross floor area or footprint, except for improvements related to fire safety, ADA accessibility, or utilities. (4) The accessory structure may be converted to residential use notwithstanding nonconformity with dimensional requirements, provided that the conversion does not increase the degree of nonconformity. (5) The accessory structure must be and remain located on the same lot. (6) The exterior façade of the accessory structure shall substantially retain its appearance and architectural features shall be preserved to the maximum extent practicable. (7) The construction of any residential unit must be in conformity with the State Building Code, Title V of the State Sanitary Code, 527 CMR – MA Fire Prevention Regulations and other local ordinances and regulations. (8) Prior to issuance of a permit, a floor plan must be submitted showing the proposed interior and exterior changes to the building. (9) For dwellings to be served by on-site septic system, the owner must obtain a letter from the Board of Health stating that the existing sewage disposal system is adequate for the proposed residential use before a Building Permit can be obtained. (10) In order to encourage the development of housing units for disabled and handicapped individuals and persons with limited mobility, the Inspector of Buildings or Zoning Board of Appeals may allow reasonable deviation from the stated conditions where necessary to install features that facilitate access and mobility for disabled persons. (11) Adaptive residential reuse of accessory structures shall not be used for short-term rentals. Pedroli at 11:11 am, Nov 19, 2026 NOTICE OF CABLE TELEVISION PUBLIC HEARING Please take notice that the Board of Selectmen of the Town of Hopedale, Massachusetts, as Issuing Authority for a cable television license under M.G.L. c.166A, will hold a public hearing on December 14, 2026 at 7:00 p.m. The public hearing will be held in The Draper Room at 54 Hopedale Street. The purpose of the public hearing will be to determine whether to issue a cable television license to Verizon/Comcast. All applications, reports, statements and license drafts to be considered at the hearing that constitute public records under state law are available for public inspection during regular business hours and for reproduction at a reasonable fee. text: Marshfield Zoning Board of Appeals 870 Moraine Street, Marshfield, MA 02050 TUESDAY, December 22, 2026 at 6:30 P.M. NOTICE OF PUBLIC HEARING Pursuant to Chapter 2 of the Acts of 2023 dated March 29, 2023, An Act Relative to Extending Certain COVID 19 Measures Adopted During the State of Emergency regarding suspending certain provisions of the Open Meeting Law, G. L. c. 30A §18, the Town of Marshfield’s Zoning Board of Appeals Meeting will be conducted both in-person and via remote participation. For this meeting, members of the public may attend in-person or may participate remotely, a hybrid form of meeting, also utilizing the ZOOM Meeting Instructions (video and phone in instructions) listed below. The public may also view the meeting by viewing the Town of Marshfield’s government access channels: Verizon (Chanel 35) and Comcast (Channel 15). Every effort will be made to ensure that members and the public can adequately access the proceedings to the best of our technical abilities; and, despite our best efforts, this meeting may be viewed as a video recording on Marshfield Community Television website (marshfieldtv.org) and a transcript or other comprehensive record of the meeting will be available as soon as possible after the meeting. title: Planning Board Public Hearing - Mount Holyoke College Geothermal Hub - Dunlap Pl (8)
text: DIANE SUPCZAK-MULVANEY, Chair BOB SZKLARZ, Vice Chair BRAD HUTCHISON, Clerk LINDA GOUIN, Member JOHN MULLIN, Member VACANT, Associate Member Anne Capra, Director of Planning & Conservation acapra@southhadleyma.gov TOWN OF SOUTH HADLEY PLANNING BOARD NOTICE OF HYBRID PUBLIC HEARING Mount Holyoke College Geothermal Hub – 8 Dunlap Place The Planning Board will hold a hybrid public hearing on December 7, 2026 at 6:30 pm. to consider applications for Site Plan Review and Stormwater Management Permit filed by Mount Holyoke College c/o Karla Youngblood; 50 College St, South Hadley, MA 01075; for the construction of a new Geothermal Hub located at 8 Dunlap Place (also known as 6 Dunlap Place), Map 49 Parcel 30. The application is being filed pursuant to South Hadley Zoning Bylaw Chapter 200 (Stormwater Management); Chapter 255 Article XII (Site Plan Review); and the Zoning Use and Dimensional Regulation Schedules. The public hearing will be held through hybrid format with in-person attendance to be located in the multipurpose room of the South Hadley Senior Center, 45 Dayton Street South Hadley MA 01075. Virtual attendance will be hosted through the log-in information below: URL to join: https://us02web.zoom.us/j/88459199447?pwd=ENpZonGHao9MyPU1qg4mobEgkiKvTN.1 Or join by phone: +1 (305) 224 1968 Webinar ID: 884 5919 9447 Passcode: 441371 The subject property includes an existing developed parking area adjacent to the Kendall Sports & Dance Complex and is located within the Residential A-1 zoning district. The application proposes to develop an approximately 5,500 square foot mechanical plant to support newly installed geothermal bore field, and the hot and chilled water distribution systems. The project also includes associated site improvements, installation of a new underground stormwater detention system, new electrical infrastructure, and underground utility connections linking the geothermal field and Geothermal Hub to the existing campus heating plant through the campus distribution piping network. The application is on file in the Planning & Conservation Department Office (Room U6) in Town Hall and is posted at www.southhadley.org on the Planning Department page under ‘Permit Applications’- ‘Site Plan Review’ under section ‘Dunlap Place (8) - Mount Holyoke Geothermal Project’ or can be viewed at: https://www.southhadley.org/1179/Site-Plan-Review. Any person interested in, or wishing to be heard, should appear/join the hearing at the time and in the manner designated. text: Town of Groton Meeting Notice Town Clerk 173 Main Street Groton, MA 01450 (978) 448-1100 Conservation Commission Meeting Wednesday, December 2 2026 at 6:00 PM The Groton Center, 163 West Main Street Groton, MA This meeting was posted Monday, November 23 2026 at 10:42 AM Agenda GROTON'S OPEN SPACE & RECREATION COMMUNITY FORUM Wednesday, December 2nd, 2026 from 6:00 PM to 8:00 PM at The Groton Center 163 Main Street, Groton MA, 01450 The Town of Groton is inviting residents and community members to participate in an upcoming Open Space and Recreation Community Forum on Wednesday, December 2, 2026, from 6:00 to 8:00 p.m. at The Groton Center (163 West Main Street). The Town is updating its Open Space and Recreation Plan, which will guide conservation and recreation priorities for the next seven years. At the Community Forum, participants will have the opportunity to explore Groton’s existing open space and recreation resources, including conservation lands, trails, recreation properties, and natural areas. Through interactive maps and materials, attendees can share their ideas, identify opportunities and challenges, and help shape future conservation and recreation priorities. The forum will be held in an open-house, drop-in format , allowing community members to stop by anytime between 6:00 and 8:00 p.m. Whether you enjoy Groton’s trails, natural areas, recreational facilities, or scenic landscapes, your input is important! All community members are encouraged to attend, share their ideas, and help shape the future of Groton’s open space and recreation resources. To learn more about the Open Space and Recreation Plan update and stay informed about future opportunities to participate, visit https://tinyurl.com/Groton-OSRP-ProjWebpage . The listing of topics that the Chair reasonably anticipates will be discussed at the meeting is not intended as a guarantee of the topics that will have been discussed. Not all topics listed may in fact be discussed, and other topics not listed may also be brought up for discussion to the extent permitted by law.

title: Conservation Commission Public Hearing 6
text: TOWN OF UXBRIDGE CONSERVATION COMMISSION 21 SOUTH MAIN STREET UXBRIDGE, MASSACHUSETTS 01569 508-278-8600 x2020 CONSERVATION PUBLIC HEARING/MEETING NOTICES The Uxbridge Conservation Commission will hold a Public Hearing on Monday December 7, 2026 at 6:30PM in the Board of Selectmen Meeting Room, Town Hall, 21 South Main Street, Uxbridge MA, to review the following application under the MA Wetlands Protection Act (MGL Ch. 131, Sec. 40). Plans may be reviewed in the Conservation office during regular business hours or on the town’s website. Notice of Intent — Filed by Fuss and O'Neil Inc on behalf of Town of Uxbridge Public Works. The proposed Douglas Street (Route 16) Reconstruction project in Uxbridge, Massachusetts. The proposed project involves the reconstruction of approximately 1.9 miles of Douglas Street (Route 16), beginning approximately 300 feet east of the Route 146 northbound ramps and extending easterly to approximately 100 feet west of the intersection with South Main Street (Route 122). An Order of Conditions is required for the proposed work because portions of the project occur within Riverfront Area associated with Cold Spring Brook, a designated Coldwater Fisheries Resource, and Buffer Zone protected under the Massachusetts Wetlands Protection Act (M.G.L. c.131 §40) and its implementing regulations at 310 CMR 10.00. The project area is also located partially within the Town of Uxbridge’s 25- foot No Disturb Zone. The project is anticipated to result in approximately 2,044 square feet of permanent impacts and 11,330 square feet of temporary impacts to the Riverfront Area, as well as 20,219 square feet of permanent impacts and 55,471 square feet of temporary impacts to the Buffer Zone. The proposed work qualifies as a Limited Project under 310 CMR 10.53(3)(f), as it involves minor roadway improvements within an existing developed right-of-way that serves a public transportation purpose. The project has been carefully designed to minimize disturbance to adjacent resource areas and to remain largely within the existing roadway footprint, thereby meeting the intent of the Limited Project provisions for public roadway and access improvements. Submitted by Russ Holden, Chairman, Uxbridge Conservation Commission

title: Public Hearing Notice - FY2027 Tax Classification Hearing
text: Town of Falmouth Select Board Fiscal Year 2027 Tax Classification Hearing Notice The Falmouth Select Board will hold a public hearing on Monday, December 7, 2026 at 6:45 p.m. in the Old Silver/Surf Drive Program Room at the Senior Center, 780 Main Street, Falmouth, MA. Under Chapter 40, section 56 as amended by Chapter 369 of the Acts of 1982 and Chapter 79 of the acts of 1983, the Falmouth Select Board will conduct a public hearing on whether the Town of Falmouth should implement the Classification Act. At said hearing, the Select Board will hear a presentation regarding the allocation of the Fiscal 2027 tax levy which will determine the share of taxes which each property classification shall pay. The Board of Assessors shall provide all information and data relevant to making a decision of allocating the tax burden, including the fiscal effects of the available options. Per order of the Select Board Publication date: Tuesday, November 24, 2026; Town website.

To the extent the Zoning Bylaw is amended with provisions that are more restrictive in their regulation of unmanned aircraft systems operation than the regulations below (e.g., a general prohibition of such operations that is enacted separately from these proposed amendments), it is the intent of the residents of Westborough, through a vote of Town Meeting, that the more restrictive provision shall prevail, unless it is the official determination of the Attomey General of a court of competent jurisdiction that a prohibition of UAS Ground Operations is not allowed. In the situation where the prohibition of the use is not allowed, UAS Ground Operations shall only be permitted by Special Permit in the AE Zoning district. B. Commercial UAS Ground Operations Special Permit a. Purpose. The purpose of this Section is to establish specific land use and zoning standards for Commercial UAS Ground Operations; provide for Commercial UAS Ground Operations in appropriate locations and under appropriate conditions: and to minimize the adverse impacts of Cominercial UAS Ground Operations on adjacent properties, residential neighborhoods, schools and other places where children congregate, historic districts, and other land uses determined to be incompatible with this use. b. Definitions. For purposes of this section: Landing Area: the pad, platform, or other location on a Locus where unmanned aircraft systems land on the ground or other horizontal surface. Launch Area: the pad, mat, or other location on a Locus from which unmanned aircraft systems launch into the air from the ground or other horizontal surface. Locus: the Lot or Lots on whieh UAS Ground Operations are proposed or conducted. Neighboriig Propetties: any property within 300 feet of the property line of the ‘Locus, whether or not located in the Town of Westborough. c. Assumptions. i. Ground activities associated with Commercial UAS Ground Operations, including launch and landing, staging, loading and unloading, and battery charging and storage, generate noise, light, traffic, and fire impacts whose effects are generally concentrated on nearby Properties. ii. Evaluating the impacts of a proposed Commercial UAS Ground Operations on properties within 300 feet of the Locus corresponds to the area the Massachusetts Legislature has identified as presumptively affected by land use and zoning applications and decisions. iii. Requiring separation of 500 linear feet between Commercial UAS Ground Operations and residences, schools, child-care establishments, places where minors frequent, places of worship, and parks is comparable to the separation this Bylaw requires between marijuana establishments and residential districts, schools, child-care establishments, and places where minors frequent (G 6.7E(2)), and between adult uses and public playgrounds, parks, and recreational areas (§ 6.6D(2)(6){3]), and reflects the Town’s established judgment as to the separation appropriate between such uses and land uses with potentially incompatible impacts.

Posted By (Name): Signature: Kathleen D. Williams Kathy Williams Route 28 Design Standards, Zoning Bylaw, and Permitting Process Amendments Planning Board Kickoff Meeting December 2, 2026 Agenda  Study Area and Project Scope  Goals, Priorities, and Desired Outcomes  Roles and Responsibilities  Key Issues  Regulatory and Permitting Issues  Public and Stakeholder Engagement  Milestones, Deliverables, Review Procedures  Proposed Schedule  Questions and Next Steps Study Area  Study Area and Project Scope Source: Google Earth Study Area Source: 11/2/2021 Yarmouth Zoning Map Project Scope  Assist Town staff and the Planning Board with modifications to the Architectural & Site Design Standards, Design Review and Site Plan Review processes, Zoning Bylaw, and permitting processes to promote mixed-use development along the Route 28 corridor. Work closely with Town staff, the Planning Board, and other boards and committees, as appropriate, throughout the project to evaluate existing regulations, develop recommended amendments, and prepare the materials necessary to facilitate implementation of the proposed changes. Goals, Priorities, and Desired Outcomes  Advance goals of the 2025 Local Comprehensive Plan (LCP) and recommendations of the Route 28 Mixed-Use Regulatory Review  Support financially viable mixed-use redevelopment within the Route 28 overlay districts  Modernize and simplify the Architectural & Site Design Standards and VCOD Design Standards while retaining the design principles most important to the community  Reduce unnecessary duplication and inconsistencies among Design Review, Site Plan Review, VCOD Site Plan Review, and overlay district permitting Goals, Priorities, and Desired Outcomes (continued)  Establish clearer expectations for applicants, Town staff, review boards and committees, and the public  Respond to pending changes to Massachusetts law governing Site Plan Review  Create user-friendly standards, procedures, tables, graphics, and permitting flowcharts that facilitate consistent implementation  Provide the Planning Board with implementation-ready amendments and supporting materials that can be advanced through the appropriate adoption and Town Meeting processes Roles and Responsibilities  BSC Group: Technical analysis, draft amendments, public engagement, and day-to-day work (benchmarking, community meetings, and developer stakeholder meeting)  Town Staff: Help w/day-to-day coordination; provide feedback, staff perspective, and direction on drafts; align deliverables with Town Meeting schedule  Planning Board: Serve as key partner and policy decision-maker at each major milestone (discuss findings, alternatives, amendments, etc.)  Other Boards & Committees: Share administrative and procedural experience to shape practical recommendations (up to 3 remote meetings)  Working Together: Hold iterative review points to make policy decisions and build consensus before detailed amendment drafting Key Issues  Starting Point: The 2025 LCP's vision of focusing growth through redevelopment in sewered areas, especially Route 28  Building on Prior Work: Confirm and update the findings of BSC's Route 28 Mixed- Use Regulatory Review and Union Studio’s Feasibility Study instead of starting over  Key Issue: Development Feasibility (Some dimensional and use requirements limit what mixed-use projects can achieve) • Commercial Share: ROAD requires 50% commercial floor area; lenders finance mixed-use less readily as the commercial share rises • Density Cap: VCOD allows 16 units/acre, but developers indicated roughly 25+ units are needed for a project to pencil out • Parking: The Zoning Bylaw prohibits reducing residential parking; at 2 spaces/unit, a 1-acre test site drops from 16 units to 10 Key Issues - Example Same Site, Same Parking Lot: Raising residential parking from 1.25 to 2 spaces per unit cuts yield from 16 to 10 units Source: Union Studio, Mixed-Use Development Feasibility Study Key Issues (continued)  Key Issue: Design and Review Processes – Overlapping reviews, unclear standards, and multiple board stops reduce predictability • Multiple Stops: VCOD projects go through Design Review, Site Plan Review, and VCOD Site Plan Review; ROAD waivers need a ZBA Special Permit after Planning Board approval  Validating Priorities: Testing and ranking issues with Town staff, the Planning Board, the community, and developers Regulatory and Permitting Issues  Zoning & Feasibility: Which combination of dimensional and use changes makes mixed-use development viable while protecting design goals?  Design Standards: Should the standards be consolidated, and should they be advisory, require substantial adherence, or be mandatory?  Review Triggers & Roles: What should trigger Design Review, and how should Design Review and Site Plan Review divide responsibilities? Regulatory and Permitting Issues (continued)  Site Plan Review Objectives: What should Site Plan Review accomplish, and how can the Site Plan Review Team process and the VCOD Site Plan Review process in the Planning Board Operational Regulations be aligned to reduce the number of stops at boards and committees?  Statutory Compliance: What changes are needed to align Site Plan Review with pending changes to Massachusetts law governing Site Plan Review?  Permitting Pathways: Where can steps in the VCOD, ROAD, and HMOD1 approval processes be consolidated, re-sequenced, or removed? Public and Stakeholder Engagement  Outreach & Participation Plan: Set up at start, with Town staff and the Planning Board, to guide engagement for project (methods, groups, etc.). Ideas?  Community Meetings: Three (3) in-person community meetings (January/February, April, and June 2027)  Developer Stakeholder Meeting: In-person meeting in March 2027 to test recommendations against real-world development experience  Board & Committee Input: The Planning Board at major milestones, plus focused sessions with other boards and committees  Clear Materials, Documented Feedback: Plain-language presentations and visuals, with summaries showing how input is used Milestones, Deliverables, Review Procedures  Four Overlapping Phases Over 12 Months: Assessment; alternatives and recommendations; regulatory drafting; and finalization and implementation  Key Milestones: Kickoff, three (3) community meetings, developer meeting, Planning Board hearing, and Town Meeting  Interim Deliverables: Each phase produces working products the Planning Board can react to before final drafting  Review Procedures: Staff review first, then Planning Board, then the public, with policy decisions settled before detailed drafting  Final Package & Town Meeting: Implementation-ready materials Proposed Schedule Task # 1 Task Meetings, Public Engagement, & Coordination 1 Planning Board & Town Staff Kick-Off Meeting 1 Develop Public/Stakeholder Outreach & Participation Plan 1 Community Meeting #1 1 Developer Stakeholder Meeting 1 Community Meeting #2 1 Community Meeting #3 1 Planning Board & Other Board/Committee Coordination 1 Project Management & Staff Coordination 2 Resource Document Review & Benchmarking 2 3 Existing Conditions & Benchmarking Memorandum Design Standards 3 Draft Revised Architectural & Site Design Standards 3 Draft Amendments to Zoning Bylaw VCOD Design Standards 4 4 5 5 Zoning Bylaw Amendments Zoning Comparison Matrix Design Review & Site Plan Review Processes Recommended Revisions & Draft Zoning Bylaw Amendments 6 Streamlining Permitting Processes 6 Updated Permitting Flowcharts 7 Final Recommendations, Summary Report, & Implementation 7 Summary Report & Implementation Package 7 Planning Board Presentation & Public Hearing 7 Town Meeting Presentation 2026 NOV DEC JAN FEB MAR APR 2027 MAY JUN JUL AUG SEP OCT Questions and Next Steps Questions  What issues are the Planning Board’s top priorities?  Which peer communities should we benchmark?  Which stakeholders and outreach channels should we use?  Should anything target April 2027?  How often should we check in with the Planning Board? Next Steps  BSC will confirm work program and schedule with Town staff  Formulation of detailed Outreach & Participation Plan  Continued resource document review Recommendations in 2025 Mixed Use Analysis for further vetting/implementation Town Planner Comments – April 2026 (Updated November 2026) 1. Design Standards: Modiﬁcations to the Architectural & Site Design Standards and the VCOD Design Standards to modernize them, make them easier to implement, and possibly combining into a single set of design standards for easier implementation by both Staff, PB and Applicant. Discuss substantial adherence versus mandatory adherence to the Design Standards and keep this in mind when developing the guidelines. Consider whether Design Standards should remain advisory for commercial development south of Route 6. Consider better deﬁning what level of redevelopment or improvements requires DRC. Does the B3 industrial area need different standards where larger warehouse buildings are proposed? Benchmarking of village design standards in other communities that may be applicable to Yarmouth will be helpful. 2. Incorporation of Changes to Chapter 40A deﬁning Site Plan Review added via the Mass Wins Act – Economic Bond Bill (in Conference Committee). Our Site Plan Review Team is staff only and does not act like Planning Board VCOD SPR. It is more identiﬁcation of regulatory requirements (zoning and other regs) as well as advisory things like cleaning out existing catch basins. More of an Administrative Project Review process. VCOD SPR needs to be modiﬁed to clearly outline the Performance Standards to be met so the Planning Board can vote on each per the pending new requirements. 3. Streamline Permitting Process: Evaluate reducing the number of stops for approval for all the optional Overlay Districts. a. Reduce the number of stops to approval for VCOD projects. Consider having the PB be the SPGA to run concurrently with the VCOD SPR process. Consider not requiring a stop at both the DRC and the PB. Review the Checklist of all the extensive information required and see if can be streamlined. Revise the VCOD application process by having Applicants go through DRC (if keep) and SPR prior to coming to the Planning Board and not run through Community Development. Plans always change somewhat based on comments from DRC and SPR before it gets to the Planning Board. b. ROAD requires 2 stops - to Planning Board for aesthetics and ZBA for relief, not sure we want to modify this as the ROAD allows for so much relief. DRC gets a copy of the application and also typically has a meeting to comment which adds another layer of aesthetic review which could be eliminated. c. HMOD1 & HMOD2 goes to the DRC and the Planning Board which serves as the SPGA, so fewer stops. d. Develop ﬂowcharts for approvals through various overlay districts. 4. Zoning: Prepare zoning spreadsheet for all Route 28 zoning districts prior to start of analysis. a. Setbacks: i. Need to evaluate min/max setbacks in VC1, and in VC3 & VC4 for properties with frontage west of the Route 28/Old Main Street where the ROW changes to 80’ as the MassDOT corridor projects require strip takings. ii. Consider reductions in setbacks abutting residential to less than 20’ but retain opaque screening and plantings and ensuring no light pollution. Page 1 of 3 b. Parking: Review minimum/maximums as well as parking dimensions. Consider making uniform throughout the bylaw and allow for angled parking. Does shared parking in the VCOD make sense? Businesses are open when residents are home, more people working from home, etc. Should senior/studios/Affordable units have different parking rates or allow for ﬂexibility on standards for these uses? Parking to the side is allowed, but should we require more detailed landscaping with trees/shrubs, berm, and/or picket fence to soften the parking visibility from the public way? c. Building Height: Evaluate setting the number of stories rather than height in B2/HMOD1/VCOD to allow for taller commercial ﬁrst ﬂoor spaces and roof designs. Consider setting a minimum lot size to allow for 4-stories in VCOD. Do we want 4stories? HMOD1 allows for 4 stories on 2-acre parcels for new hotels. HMOD2 allows 4 stories for hotels. Medical Overlay District (MOD) allows for 6 stories and 85’ (very limited area near the Hospital). d. Lighting Standards: Decorative lighting is expensive, consider allowing a little taller heights to allow for fewer ﬁxtures, consider different, less expensive options in rear parking lots. Evaluate allowed heights throughout the bylaw. e. Unit Sizes: Although Affordable units have a set unit size, consider reductions in minimum unit sizes to allow for more units. There is a need for housing for singles and professional couples. Include on-site storage in unit size calculations? f. Density: The illustrative analysis done by Union Studios shows it is difficult to get up to 16 units/acre and provide 2 parking spaces/unit. If decrease unit sizes, should we increase density? Consider density as it relates to #bedrooms/acre. FAR ratios? Yarmouth is not ready for no density limits or form-based code. g. Mixed Use Commercial Percentage: Review the % of commercial space required. Should it be the % of the ground ﬂoor rather than gross ﬂoor area? Only the portion of the building facing Route 28? Consider other ways to activate ground ﬂoor uses for certain non-commercial uses, consider lobby/community room in the front, work/live space, public artist space, etc. Is 50% max. residential too high for a ROAD mixed-use project? 5. Stakeholder Meetings: Continue seeking diversiﬁed stakeholder input to include developers, property/business owners, engineers, Town Staff, etc. People in the trenches making projects happen. Ideas on how to more cost effectively build aesthetically pleasing buildings. What design standards are hardest/most expensive to implement? 6. Use Table: Retail/offices are not in demand, residential is. Should we be promoting other types of uses along Route 28 for economic diversiﬁcation? Do we want to consider light manufacturing with retail component along Route 28? Com Dev working on an RFP for a new Market Study to look at what type of uses we need. Look at modifying A11 Employee Housing at non-Motels/Hotels to allow more top of shop for workforce in general. Do we want to allow Single Family and Duplexes in the VCOD to promote cottage style development? Look at allowing duplexes by right in all districts for lots meeting current minimum lot sizes (rather than existing twice the minimum), at least in the R40 zoning district (may be moot if Econ. Bond Bill does this by-right on conforming and nonconforming lots). Do we need to further differentiate between housing types (i.e., townhome, triplex, multi-family, top of shop, etc.)? Page 2 of 3 Other recommendations which we may not want to further vet? • No Density Limits. • Smaller Lots with Reduced Frontage (Idea is to allow for individual units on smaller lots that would be for sale rather than multi-family for sale via condominiums to help with ﬁnancing.) • Full Review/Overhaul of the Use Table. • Combining the four VCOD subdistricts into one. Page 3 of 3 Approach to Work & Work Plan PROJECT UNDERSTANDING BSC understands the Town of Yarmouth is seeking to build upon the significant planning and infrastructure investments already underway along the Route 28 corridor by creating a clearer, more predictable, and more effective regulatory framework for mixed-use redevelopment. The Town’s 2025 Local Comprehensive Plan (LCP) establishes a vision for focusing future growth and redevelopment in areas served by municipal sewer infrastructure, while the Route 28 Mixed-Use Analysis identified regulatory, design, permitting, and financial considerations affecting the feasibility of mixed-use development. This project represents an important next step: translating those planning recommendations into implementable changes to the Town’s Design Standards, Zoning Bylaw, and development review processes. BSC brings a particularly strong understanding of the foundation for this effort, having prepared the Route 28 Mixed-Use Regulatory Review as part of the Town’s recent mixed-use analysis. Through that work, BSC evaluated the existing regulatory framework along Route 28, including the Village Centers Overlay District (VCOD), Revitalization Overlay Architectural District (ROAD), Hotel/Motel Overlay District 1 (HMOD1), and underlying zoning requirements. This familiarity will allow our team to efficiently transition from prior analysis to implementation while revisiting earlier findings where necessary based on input from Town staff, the Planning Board, developers, stakeholders, and the public. Our approach recognizes successful regulatory reform requires more than simply revising individual dimensional standards or permitting provisions. Design requirements, zoning regulations, development economics, and permitting procedures are interconnected. Changes to building height, setbacks, density, parking, commercial space requirements, or design standards can affect development feasibility, while overlapping review procedures or unclear approval standards can introduce uncertainty even where zoning otherwise supports redevelopment. The items to be discussed include the agenda items listed below. Mayor's Orders briefing and announcements by Mayor Vieau or designee. Public Input Communications: Minutes 11/5/26 City Council Meeting, 11/16/26 Special City Council Meeting MO-1 Whereas, the City of Chicopee has determined that there is a need in the City of Chicopee for a redevelopment authority, organized pursuant to Section 4 of Chapter 121B of the General Laws, as amended, for the purpose of engaging in urban renewal, land assembly, redevelopment projects, and other work pursuant to said Chapter 121B, and that it is in the public interest that such authority be organized in the City of Chicopee. Ordered by the City Council of the City of Chicopee that the Chicopee Redevelopment Authority be and it hereby is, organized, pursuant to said Section 4, for the purpose of engaging in urban renewal, land assembly, redevelopment projects, and other work pursuant to said Chapter 121B in the City of Chicopee, and that, pursuant to said Section 4, the appointment of said Authority and the taking of all other action necessary to the issuance by the Secretary of the Commonwealth of a certificate of organization is hereby authorized. MO-02 Be it Ordained by the City Council that the Code of the City of Chicopee for the year 1991, as amended, be and is hereby further amended as follows: Add to Chapter 16 Commissions, Committees, Councils and Authorities Article XXVII Redevelopment Authority § 16-119 Establishment and authority. There is hereby established a Chicopee Redevelopment Authority, organized pursuant to Section 4 of Chapter 121B of the Massachusetts General Laws, as amended, for the purpose of engaging in urban renewal, land assembly, redevelopment projects, and other work pursuant to said Chapter 121B. §16-120 Membership; appointment and terms. A. The Redevelopment Authority shall be managed, controlled and governed by five members, of whom three shall constitute a quorum, consistent with MGL 1218, §5. Each member of the Redevelopment Authority shall be a resident of the City of Chicopee. B. Four members of the Redevelopment Authority shall be appointed by the Mayor, subject to confirmation by the City Council, consistent with MGL 121B, §5, with staggered terms starting at five years, four years, two years, and one year, with each member having five-year terms following the expiration of the initial term. C. One member of the Redevelopment Authority shall be appointed by the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities, consistent with MGL 121B, § 5, for an initial term of three years, with the member having five-year terms following the expiration of the initial term. §16-121 Removal of members; vacancies. A. Members of the Redevelopment Authority may resign or be removed consistent with MGL 121B, § 6. B. Vacancies, other than by reason of expiration of terms, shall be filled for the balance of the unexpired term, in the same manner and by the same body as for the vacated member. Every member, unless sooner removed, shall serve until the qualifications of a successor. §16-122 Powers and duties; staff. A. The Redevelopment Authority shall have all the powers and duties as outlined in Chapter 121B of the General Laws, as amended, and said Authority may employ counsel, an executive director and such other officers, agents and employees as it deems necessary or proper, subject to the appropriation therefor. B. So far as practicable, the Redevelopment Authority shall make use of the services of the agencies, officers and employees of the City of Chicopee, and the City shall, if requested, make available such services, consistent with MGL 121B, § 7. MO-3 Ordered that the City Council accept the Underutilized Properties Program Grant in the amount of Two hundred fifty thousand and 00/100 dollars ($250,000.00) from Massdevelopment. This grant was awarded for pre-development work at the Uniroyal Redevelopment Parcel located at 154 Grove Street to support private redevelopment of the property. Said grant is accepted in accordance with M.G.L. Chapter 44 Section 53A. MO-4 Mayor's appropriation of Two hundred fifty thousand and 00/100 dollars ($250,000.00) to the following named account: Planning Special Account for Uniroyal Infrastructure Improvements from available funds in the Stabilization Fund. MO-5 Mayor's appropriation of Two hundred twenty-one thousand eight hundred fifty and 00/100 dollars ($221,850.00) to the following named account: Fire Special Account for Purchase Fire Dept Ambulances from available funds in the Stabilization for Capital Budgeting. M0-6 Mayor's appropriation of Fifty-five thousand and 00/100 dollars ($55,000.00) to the following named account: Fire Special Account for Vehicle Purchases from available funds in the Stabilization for Capital Budgeting. Holiday Recycling Collection Schedule A. Purpose and Intent. The purpose of this section is to provide residents with additional convenient curbside recycling opportunities during the holiday season, when households traditionally generate increased quantities of cardboard, packaging, and other recyclable materials. This section is intended to improve the convenience and accessibility of municipal recycling services through a limited seasonal adjustment to the existing collection schedule, while preserving yard waste collection and minimizing disruption to the operations of the Department of Public Works. B. Holiday Recycling Collection. Notwithstanding the regular biweekly recycling collection schedule established pursuant to § 223-5{A), the Department of Public Works shall provide curbside recycling collection during each of the following two consecutive calendar weeks: 1. The calendar week in which December 25 occurs; and 2. The calendar week immediately following the week in which December 25 occurs. These two consecutive weeks shall be designated as recycling collection weeks for all properties receiving municipal curbside recycling services. For purposes of this section, a calendar week shall begin on Sunday and end on Saturday, consistent with the municipal collection schedule established under§ 169-12. C. Preservation of Yard Waste and Christmas Tree Collection. To minimize disruption to existing yard waste collection services, the Department of Public Works shall establish the following four-week collection rotation: 1. Week preceding Christmas week: Yard waste collection. 2. Christmas week: Recycling collection. 3. Week immediately following Christmas week: Recycling collection. 4. Week immediately following the second recycling week: Yard waste collection, including Christmas trees. The four-week rotation shall preserve two recycling collection weeks and two yard waste collection weeks within the designated period. The Department of Public Works shall incorporate any necessary adjustments into the annual collection calendar to accommodate this rotation while maintaining the regular aiternating schedule during the remainder of the year. Nothing in this section shall prohibit the continued operation of existing yard waste dropoff services or the establishment of additional voluntary disposal opportunities for residents. D. Staffing and Operational Considerations. The holiday collection schedule shall be implemented through adjustments to the existing recycling and yard waste collection rotation. Nothing in this section shall require the Department of Public Works to: 1. Conduct recycling and yard waste collections simultaneously during the same calendar week; 2. Establish additional weekly collection routes solely for the purpose of implementing this section; or 3. Alter regularly scheduled municipal household trash collection services. The Superintendent of Public Works shall retain responsibility for determining staffing assignments, equipment utilization, collection routes, and other operational procedures necessary to implement the designated collection schedule. E. Publication and Public Notification. The Department of Public Works shall incorporate the holiday collection schedule into its regularly published annual curbside collection calendar. The Department shall clearly identify the two consecutive holiday recycling weeks and the designated yard waste collection weeks using the existing calendar format. The Department shall also provide reasonable public notification of the seasonal adjustment through established municipal communication channels, including the City's website and other customary public notices. All regularly applicable holiday collection delays shall remain in effect pursuant to§ 169- 12. F. Implementation and Evaluation. The holiday collection schedule established by this section shall first be implemented during the 2028 holiday season, continuing into January 2029. The Department of Public Works shall evaluate the initial implementation, including any significant operational challenges, resident inquiries, and effects on recycling and yard waste collection, and provide a brief summary of its findings to the City Council following the conclusion of the initial holiday collection period. G. Effective Date. This ordinance shall take effect on January 1, 2028. Nothing herein shall require modification or reprinting of the previously established 2027 municipal curbside collection calendar. 39 An application for a NEW Special Permit under Section 275-58 C4/C5 of the Municipal Zoning Ordinance for the purpose of application for on premise liquor license and one residential unit in a business building. Pledge of Allegiance and Moment of Silence: Act on Minutes: On motion made by Councilor Markee and seconded by Councilor Schmidt it was unanimously voted to approve the minutes of March 18, 2026 and April 8, 2026. Public Comment Summary: President Denham stated that each speaker would have three minutes to address the Council on any item not listed under the public hearing. Richard McNeil, 54 Oliver Street, stated that he and his wife live across from the town farm, which was dedicated to the inhabitants of Easthampton 136 years ago and carries deed restrictions covering the homestead, the farmland, and affordable supportive housing for people in transition. He stated that the homestead and land should be kept together, and spoke in support of a collaboration between the Farmer Veteran Coalition and Renewal Initiatives that he said intends to restore the farmland and homestead, provide agricultural training and housing for veterans, and support the Chicoine family farm. Cathy Wauczinski, Overlook Drive, spoke against the proposed override. She stated that the budget situation should not be described as a surprise, citing staff hour reductions, draws on stabilization funds, and months of discussion of health insurance costs during last year's budget process, and that the City Council should have reviewed the budget more thoughtfully in prior years. Elizabeth Cocco, 74 Oliver Street, stated that housing should be returned to 75 Oliver Street as fully occupied affordable housing, that the land should continue to honor its farming legacy, that the housing and land should remain together, and that any proposal selected must have the financial strength and long-term commitment to sustain the property. President Denham reminded speakers that 75 Oliver Street was on the public hearing agenda and that comments on that item should be made during the hearing. Paul Dise, Willow Circle, spoke regarding the budget. He stated that from FY24 to FY26 budgeted school spending and the total budget increased 8.5 percent while the Social Security cost-of-living adjustment averaged 2.8 percent; that full-time equivalent employees increased from 376 in FY22 to 435 in FY25, a 16 percent increase; and asked where the City's $6.1 million in COVID relief funds went and whether any became permanent expenditures. He stated that 1 approximately 25 percent of residents are 65 or older and on fixed incomes, and asked the Council to control spending rather than raise taxes, noting that voters have approved three overrides for buildings. Carol Brodeur, 72 Oliver Street, spoke against the proposed rent control, stating that landlords' costs for insurance and upkeep rise just as the City's costs do and that rent control would result in substandard housing. She also stated that she opposes the override. She noted that overlapping meeting times make it difficult for residents to attend multiple meetings. On motion made by Councilor Kwiecinski and seconded by Councilor Schmidt it was unanimously voted to open the Public Hearing. Public Hearings starting at 6:15 p.m. Supplemental Appropriation: $29,907.49 from Free Cash to fund equipment necessary to support computer systems (continued from April 22, 2026) Councilor Peake stated that he was not present at the previous meeting and understood that the Council was awaiting additional information from the Technology Director. Dr. Karin Camihort, Technology Director (online), stated that the request would establish a secondary location for the city's data center so that the city could switch over immediately if the data center became unavailable due to a fire or cyberattack, and would also allow the city to age its equipment gradually and test updates. She stated that if the request is not approved, the alternative would be to move disaster recovery to a cloud system such as Microsoft Azure at roughly $600 per month to maintain, rising to around $8,000 per month if the city had to run its systems from the cloud during a disaster. Councilor Schmidt asked whether grant funds would be lost if the request were not approved. Dr. Camihort stated that they would not, and that the city would look for grants in the future and for ways for the city and School Department, which both have aging systems, to share resources. Councilor Smith asked whether the Technology Department had looked into sharing costs with nearby communities, as a resident suggested at the last meeting. Dr. Camihort said the city had spoken with South Hadley and other towns, but there would be a cost, and running on another community's environment would mean less control over cybersecurity and access to confidential data. She stated that the first step should be to work with the school system. Councilor Peake asked how the risk of a cloud-based solution compared with a physical secondary location. Dr. Camihort stated that risk is always higher when systems are exposed to the internet; that a local secondary data center would communicate fiber to fiber internally and would not be reachable from the internet; but that she is confident Azure would be a safe option and that the city could be up and running within a couple of hours to a day. 2 Vice-President Jadczak asked whether the city is locked into Azure and whether the $8,000 monthly cost would be prorated. Dr. Camihort stated that the city has no contract with Azure, that Azure is the least expensive option because the city is a Windows environment, and that the cost is pay-as-you-go, which could be further reduced by running only essential systems and powering some down during off hours. She noted that the city's cybersecurity insurance should cover some of these costs in the event of a cyberattack. Councilor Jamrog-McQuaid asked about the lifespan of the equipment. Dr. Camihort stated that the city buys important systems with five years of support for parts, which is less expensive than buying support year to year, and in response to a follow-up question confirmed that the requested amount includes the service agreements for hardware, parts, support, and patches. President Denham and Councilor Smith confirmed that the choice was between paying $29,907.49 now and paying $600 per month, plus disaster costs, for the cloud option. Councilor Peake noted that $600 per month over five years would total $36,000, about $6,093 more than the requested appropriation, for a system he believes would be somewhat less secure, assuming the cloud price does not increase. Councilor Newton asked whether the system would be large enough to connect the schools. Dr. Camihort stated that those conversations have not started, but that the servers would have enough capacity and some additional storage might be needed. Councilor Kwiecinski asked whether the Council would be short-sighted not to consider a combined city and school system first. Dr. Camihort stated that integrating the departments will take time, that about half of Massachusetts communities run city and school IT separately and half merged, and that a response would take at least a month. In response to Councilor Peake, she confirmed that the chassis would be sufficient and only additional storage might be needed if the schools joined, noting that the schools also use a Windows and VMware environment with direct fiber connectivity. In response to Councilor Schmidt, she stated that the Mayor has directed her to pursue integration with the schools regardless of which option is chosen. Chris O'Connor, Ashley Circle, asked whether a risk analysis had been done of which systems must be restored and in what time frame, including for the schools. Dr. Camihort stated that the city has a plan identifying the most important systems, that recovery depends on the type of disaster, and that the city keeps static backups old enough to restore from a point before an undetected infiltration, noting that the department has two and a half staff and no dedicated cybersecurity experts. Cathy Wauczinski, Overlook Drive, asked what would happen if the city did nothing, and whether the city should use the less expensive monthly option while it explores merging with the school district and grant funding. Dr. Camihort stated that the city currently has no secondary backup, that the level of risk is high, and that a secondary location was the top recommendation of the city's incident response planning and two tabletop exercises. She 3 stated that the Azure option is not ideal but would be safe enough until more funding becomes available. Jess Atkins-Barber, 22 Vadnais Street, encouraged the Council to approve the transfer, stating that an off-site backup follows the 3-2-1 backup rule, that a city-owned server would be less expensive and safer than Azure, citing past outages at major cloud providers, and that adding storage later for the schools would not be a major expense. Leslie Button (online) asked how frequently the city's data is backed up. Dr. Camihort stated that the financial and public safety systems are backed up every six hours, domain controllers once a week, and most other systems once a day. Eileen Jager, 80 Williston Avenue, stated that she agreed with the previous speaker and Councilor Peake that investing in city-owned hardware in a known location would be more controllable than a cloud service whose prices could increase. President Denham acknowledged the participation of Easthampton High School students in the meeting. Councilor Schmidt asked where the funding for the rest of the project would come from. Dr. Camihort said it would come from ARPA funds. Councilor Smith asked for an estimate of the cost of additional storage for the schools. Dr. Camihort stated that she could not estimate it without knowing the schools' needs, but that the system includes room to grow and adding disks is less expensive than buying a new server. On motion by Councilor Peake and seconded by Councilor Kwiecinski it was unanimously voted to approve the following appropriation: amount requested $29,907.49 to be transferred from Free Cash. The requested appropriation of $29,907.49 will be applied towards a portion of the total $59,446.90 cost of the city's disaster recovery infrastructure project, which includes two PowerEdge R670 servers ($41,958.70) and one PowerVault ME5224 storage system ($17,488.20). This equipment is necessary to support timely recovery of the city's critical onpremises systems in the event of a hardware failure, cybersecurity incident, or prolonged outage, and to reduce the risk of disruptions to essential municipal operations and services. Referral for disposition and Resolution to declare surplus and dispose of the Town Lodging House, 75 Oliver Street (continued from April 22, 2026) President Denham stated that the Council would first discuss the resolution to declare the property surplus and authorize its disposal, and then the Request for Proposals (RFP), and reminded those present that the property carries three deed restrictions: affordable housing, historic preservation, and agricultural preservation. Councilor Kwiecinski, Chair of the Property Committee, explained that an RFP is a formal legal process by which the City advertises the terms and conditions that any proposal must meet, and that the Council's role is to come to an agreement with the Mayor on whether to dispose of the property and under what conditions. 4 Councilor Markee asked whether the declaration of surplus or the RFP would determine whether the property is divided. Allyson Manuel, Planning Director, stated that the City is not proposing to divide the property, which is a single parcel including the farmland, outbuildings, and lodging house, and that both the resolution and the RFP as drafted keep it together. Councilor Peake asked whether the RFP would preclude a joint proposal from two parties, one interested in the housing and one in the agricultural land. Planning Director Manuel stated that it would not; the RFP only precludes a proposal that addresses agriculture or housing alone. Zoom Login instructions: Instructions and the meeting link for this specific meeting can be found at the following web address: http://www.falmouthma.gov/Conservation Please plan on 10-15 minutes of preparation time to log in though it may be less if you have previously used Zoom on the device you will use to access this meeting. Additionally public comments may be sent in advance of the meeting to concom@falmouthma.gov at least 5 hours prior to the beginning of the meeting. Documents and audio or video files may also be submitted via email. Submitted email comments and documents will be made part of the meeting record. Applicants, their representatives and individuals with enforcement matters before the Conservation Commission shall appear remotely. Applicants, their representatives and individuals with enforcement matters before the Conservation Commission may contact the Conservation Department to arrange an alternative means of real time participation if unable to use the Zoom virtual meeting software. Go to www.fatv.org/watch-fatv for more information on accessing this meeting. This is intended to help you understand the meeting format and assist you with the rules of the Council as they pertain to your participation. All meetings of the Fitchburg City council are open to the public. This does not mean that the public participates in all aspects of the meeting. It simply means that the meeting itself, including all discussions and votes, is open for public view. Executive Session The only time a Council meeting can be closed to the public is when the Council votes for Executive Session in order to discuss sensitive matters in private, such as pending litigation. Any votes taken however, must be taken in open session. OPPORTUNITIES FOR THE PUBLIC TO SPEAK DURING A COUNCIL MEETING: Public Forum The Public Forum occurs immediately following the Pledge of Allegiance. The President will ask if anyone in the audience wishes to speak on any matter appearing on the Agenda. If you wish to address the Council, you must stand and be recognized and follow these rules before speaking: 1. 2. 3. 4. State your name and city of residence. Approach the center table and either stand or sit. This allows you to be seen and heard clearly by everyone in attendance. You may speak only on items appearing on the agenda for no more than (2) minutes. Copies of the agenda are available on the center table prior to the meeting. Please state the petition, order, ordinance, or resolution number to which you refer. Public Hearings Public hearings are held on various issues such as Special Permits and Zoning changes.
